claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 exhibits a hierarchical heterostructure containing nanoscale or microscale phase domains, compositional gradients, or precipitate distributions.
High-resolution SEM or TEM imaging can characterize the hierarchical heterostructure of HfNbTiVAl10.
Supervised machine-learning models trained on experimental tensile and fracture data can predict the mechanical properties of HfNbTiVAl10.
Domain size, phase distribution, and interface density can be extracted as image-derived descriptors of the hierarchical heterostructure.
Machine-learning models can directly correlate image-derived heterostructural features with mechanical outcomes.
Using image-derived features and machine learning bypasses the need for detailed physical simulation of complex heterostructures.
Bypassing detailed physical simulation will improve prediction speed.
Directly capturing heterostructural features and statistically correlating them with measured properties will improve predictive accuracy.
The proposed method will predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior at least twice as fast as established finite-element or molecular-dynamics simulations.
The proposed method will reduce mean absolute prediction error by 20–30% relative to established simulation methods.
The claimed gains apply to tensile and fracture tests conducted at ambient temperature and laboratory-typical strain rates.
The comparator consists of finite-element or molecular-dynamics simulations using generic microstructural assumptions or simplified models.
The method may fail when imaging does not adequately capture the hierarchical heterostructure.
The method may fail when the training dataset is insufficiently representative.
The method may fail when behavior is dominated by atomic-scale defects or local chemistry that is not visible in the imaging data.
The magnitude of the accuracy gain depends on the quality and representativeness of the imaging and training data.
Accuracy gains may be smaller for properties that are highly sensitive to atomic-scale effects.
